newsitem.title: USA: U.S. East Coast sees record power demand.
newsitem.headline: U.S. East Coast sees record power demand.

text.p: Hot weather toppled records for electricity demand up and down the U.S. East Coast Tuesday as air conditioners groaned through the muggy afternoon.
"We hit a new peak for the Con Edison system at 4:00 PM (1600 EDT) of 11,013 megawatts," said Patrick Wheeler, a spokesman for Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc.
The previous record of 10,805 MW, set August 2, 1995, fell as the thermometer in Central Park registered a withering 98 degrees Fahrenheit.

"Unfortunately, we've had some localized problems. We still have about 600 customers out of service in Yonkers due to some cable failures, and we have a voltage reduction in parts of Brooklyn," he said.

The Brooklyn problems were also blamed on feeder cables, which forced ConEd to cut voltage by eight percent to some neighborhoods and prompted a plea to customers to turn off all unneeded lights and appliances, especially air conditioners, to "avoid possible loss of service".
ConEd serves some 2.9 million customers in New York City and suburban Westchester County.
The surging demand was also felt in upstate New York and New England.
"Continued hazy, hot, humid weather throughout New York State has driven customer demand for electricity to record levels today," the New York Power Pool (NYPP) said in a statement.
The pool, which oversees operation of the state's power grid, said demand peaked at 1500 EDT at 28,700 megawatts (MW), surpassing the previous high of 27,206 MW set August 4, 1995.

Across the Hudson in neighboring New Jersey, Newark-based Public Service Electric and Gas Co (PSE&G) confirmed it moved a record 9,612 megawatts (MW) across its system at 1400 EDT, surpassing the previous high of 9,470 MW, also set on August 2, 1995.

The New England Power Pool, while today falling a bit short of Monday's record 20,534 MW load, said they were declaring Wednesday a "conservation day" and asking customers to throttle back on power usage.
The soaring demand was seen in soaring prices.

Spot electricity for peak next-day delivery was traded across much of the East Coast at over $100 per megawatt hour, with prices in the Southeast hitting a staggering $170, compared with an already lofty $62 the day before.
"Power prices are screaming," said one trader, adding he had never seen next-day power prices this high.

Meteorologists are calling for some relief Wednesday, when thundershowers are forecast for parts of the region. But temperatures are expected to stay in the 90s for most of the week, ensuring continued high air conditioning demand.
